items.title: Researchers propose Cache-to-Cache, a direct semantic communication method between large language models using KV-cache fusion, improving accuracy by up to 14.2% and reducing latency by 2.5x [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Cache-to-Cache: Direct Semantic Communication Between LLMs (2025)
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Cache-to-Cache (C2C), a new approach enabling large language models (LLMs) to communicate directly through fused KV-cache representations instead of text, preserving richer semantic information and reducing latency. Experiments show C2C improves average accuracy by 6.4-14.2% over individual models and outperforms traditional text-based communication by 3.1-5.4%, while delivering a 2.5x speedup in response time.

C2C uses a neural network to project and combine the source model's KV-cache with the target model's cache, employing a learnable gating mechanism to select beneficial layers for communication. This method avoids token-by-token generation delays and leverages deep, specialized semantics from both models, offering a more efficient and effective multi-LLM system design. The researchers have made their code publicly available for further exploration and development.

items.title: NASA and IBM release open-source Lunar Foundation Model combining multimodal lunar datasets for scientific analysis with USRA planetary science expertise [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation open-Source Geospatial AI Model
items.summary:
NASA and IBM Research have developed the NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model, an open-source artificial intelligence model pretrained on SomBench, a multimodal lunar dataset with nearly two million data bundles across 11 modalities. The model integrates diverse lunar data such as imagery, topography, mineralogy, and environmental properties to support scientific analysis of the Moon. The Universities Space Research Association (USRA) contributed planetary science expertise, dataset development, and evaluation to the project, with Dr. Rachel Slank serving as a subject-matter expert connecting lunar science priorities to model development.

The model was evaluated on benchmarks including crater detection, segmentation of irregular mare patches, and lunar polar ice prospectivity regression, matching or outperforming comparison models and demonstrating strong label efficiency. Its multimodal design enables learning relationships among different lunar observations at both regional and meter scales. By releasing the pretrained model, fine-tuning code, and benchmark datasets openly, the team aims to provide a reusable foundation for lunar research applications and advance machine learning methods in planetary science.

items.title: Author outlines two rules for using large language models to improve writing without losing personal voice [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How to Write with an LLM
items.summary:
The article advises writers to first draft their work independently and then use large language models (LLMs) as copyeditors rather than ghostwriters. It emphasizes two key rules: never use exact phrases suggested by LLMs and avoid accepting their encouragement, as these can dilute the writer's unique voice and lead to unnatural, overly polished text.

The author explains that while LLMs excel at identifying issues like passive voice overuse, repetitive phrases, and misplaced paragraphs, relying too heavily on their suggestions can result in writing that feels artificial. Instead, writers should use LLMs to flag problems and guide revisions without adopting their specific wording or positive feedback, preserving authenticity and clarity in their prose.

Researchers at Cornell University analyzed around 20,000 AI-generated stories and found that names like Elias and occupations like lighthouse keeper appeared in a majority of them, despite no clear source for the character's origin.

The persistence of Elias Thorne is believed to result from AI safety and alignment training that limits the models' access to copyrighted or sensitive material, leading to a narrower pool of data for story generation. Additionally, AI models often train on outputs from earlier models, causing repeated recycling of the same fictional elements. This phenomenon highlights the limited diversity and originality in AI-generated content due to constrained training data and iterative reuse of prior AI outputs.

items.title: IncoAI launches Splash, an open-source inference engine optimized for Apple silicon that doubles decode speed on Qwen3.8-27B and supports up to 32K tokens [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Splash: A Local Engine Built Around the Model
items.summary:
IncoAI has introduced Splash, an open-source inference engine designed specifically for Apple silicon Macs running macOS 26.4 or later with at least 36 GB of unified memory. Unlike typical inference engines built for flexibility, Splash is specialized around individual models, delivering up to twice the decode speed of the next-fastest engine on the Qwen3.8-27B model and nearly four times faster with four parallel subagents. It supports streaming, tool calls, JSON Schema output, and image input through standard APIs.

Splash's architecture includes fused shape-specific kernels, trained draft models, and optimized memory management tailored to each supported model. It uses speculative decoding as a core feature, with each model shipping its own trained draft to accelerate token prediction. The engine manages memory dynamically, balancing prefill and decode workloads while reusing cached attention states to improve efficiency. Splash is integrated with LM Studio Bionic, enabling fast, local inference for agentic applications on Macs without additional configuration.

items.title: Report: Google AI Studio's 'Delete' button hides prompts instead of deleting them, contradicting user warnings and potentially violating GDPR [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Google AI Studio 'Delete' is a scam: Your prompts are not deleted, just hidden
items.summary:
A security researcher alleges that Google AI Studio does not actually delete user prompts when the 'Delete' button is clicked but only hides them by removing a shortcut file, leaving the data active on Google's servers. The researcher claims this practice contradicts Google's own documentation and user interface warnings, which state that deletion is permanent and unrecoverable. The researcher also reports that Google banned their bug bounty account after they disclosed this issue, labeling it as intended behavior.

The researcher points to Google's Help Center admitting that an automated tool can recover 'permanently deleted' files, which conflicts with the notion of permanent deletion. They argue this constitutes deceptive design and a violation of European data protection laws, specifically GDPR Article 17, which requires actual data erasure. The researcher provided forensic evidence but says Google dismissed the findings and took no corrective action.

This controversy raises questions about user data privacy and transparency in AI tools, with potential legal implications for Google. It also highlights challenges in verifying data deletion claims in cloud services and the effectiveness of bug bounty programs in addressing such concerns.

items.originalTitle: Communicate Technical Topics to a Non-Technical Audience with Google Gemini
items.summary:
In a room full of IT professionals, words and phrases like “tokenization,” “retrieval-augmented generation,” and “context window” need no explanation. But when technology leaders present to their CEOs and other company leaders about topics like AI, they often find that they need to translate these terms into everyday business language, or else risk being met by blank stares.

In the moment, this can be maddening. You know the opportunities and challenges that a technology like generative AI presents for your company. And you know that the organization’s other leaders will likely see things the same way you do, if only you can make yourself understood.

Instead of trying to bridge this communication gap on the fly, use Google Gemini to help translate your technical vision into bottom-line business value.

Step 1: Figure Out What You Want to Say

Your CEO might not speak “tech,” but Google Gemini does. Open up a new chat and explain exactly what it is you hope to communicate to leadership. Here, you can feel free to be as technical as you wish. Maybe you’ll tell Gemini that you’re thinking of building a RAG pipeline to vectorize your company’s proprietary data. Or, maybe you’ll float the idea of using parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA to deploy open-weight models on-premises, without exploding your cloud inference costs. You can even upload your technical documents to Gemini, directly in the chat window.

No matter how in-the-weeds you get, Gemini will follow your train of thought, parsing the complexity to find the business value at the core of your plans.

Step 2: Let Gemini Be Your Translator

Now that you’ve captured your vision in your own words, let Gemini help you translate those words into language that will connect with your audience. Use this sample prompt, along with your brainstorming from Step 1:

I am the CIO at [company], and I am trying to build the case to [adopt generative AI solutions]. I need to explain the technical concept of generative AI to a non-technical audience (the CEO and board). Help me write talking points that will help me convey what generative AI is, ways it could help us digitally transform, and why it’s important to our growth as a company. Include details about how it could potentially re-focus our technical talent on more strategic work, help enhance our workforce’s productivity, and help us better serve our global workforce and customers.

In just a few moments, you’ll have a set of boardroom-ready talking points. Gemini might, for instance, break down the benefits of RAG in simple terms by noting that it anchors AI to internal data like HR policies and technical manuals. Or, it might point out the business benefits of arming IT staff and engineers with generative AI tools, noting the opportunity to shift employees’ focus from low-value, repetitive tasks to innovation.

Step 3: Create Content


Now that you have your core narrative and language nailed down, Gemini can help you create a more structured pitch. Instead of staring at a blank slide deck, prompt Gemini for ideas on how to build out a presentation that will sway your peers in the C-suite. Try this prompt:

I need to build a presentation to deliver this information to the board. Turn these talking points into a 10-slide presentation. For each slide, write a headline, three to four short bullet points for the slide itself, and the speaker notes I should use to explain the concept out loud.

Gemini will generate a full, downloadable presentation deck directly in the chat. If you like, you can export the presentation to Google Slides and make your own edits. Or, you can command Gemini to generate a new version with changes to elements like design, language, and narrative flow.

Step 4: Make Gemini Your Sparring Partner

Before you go into your meeting, open a new chat in Gemini, providing your speaker notes and a link to your presentation, and then ask it to act as a skeptical executive: You are my CEO. Review this presentation and grill me on cost, security, and ROI. Ask your toughest questions, one at a time.

Even though Gemini helped you prepare your presentation, it will seamlessly pivot to the role of rigorous executive or tough board member, pressing for more details on project payback, hidden risks, and timeline. By practicing your pitch in this low-stakes environment, you can make certain that you’ll be confident when it’s time for the real thing.
